country.evidence_source: [/page/4/Text/4] Chinese people tend to define children's achievements primarily in terms of academic achievement (Stevenson & Lee, 1996). One of the main criteria for an ideal child among Chinese parents is his or her academic attributes, such as the child's academic performance and attitude toward academic work (Shek & Chan, 1999). One likely reason that educational attainment is highly valued among Chinese is its functional value to one's future. Chinese parents believe that high academic achievement is an effective means for their children to achieve a bright future and a rewarding career (Chen et al., 1996; Leung, Salili, & Baber, 1986). Despite such a great emphasis on academic attainment, advanced education and university facilities can only be provided to a relatively small proportion of the population because of the limited resources in Hong Kong (Leung et al., 1986). Thus, there is keen academic competition from kindergarten to high school among Chinese children (Stevenson & Lee, 1996).

Outcome_variable.evidence_source: [/page/4/Text/4] The other measured predictor of life satisfaction in this study was perceived academic competence. [/page/5/Text/2] success and failure in school examinations affect students'subjective well-being (Hu, 1994; Lau, Siu, & Chik, 1998). [/page/5/Text/3] Reviews of Western studies consistently support the idea that children's life satisfactions directly vary with their academic self-concepts, which are subjective evaluations of one's academic competence (Dew & Huebner, 1994; Huebner, Gilman, & Laughlin, 1999; Terry & Huebner, 1995). Similarly, a positive relation has been found between academic self-concept and life satisfaction among junior high school children from Hong Kong (Leung & Leung, 1992; Leung & Zhang, 2000).

Given these great academic pressures, perceived academic competence was hypothesized to be a significant positive predictor of early adolescents' life satisfactions.
